title: Five Hundred Copies, and Thirty Years of Nobody Listening
standfirst: Three brothers in Detroit pressed five hundred copies of a single and then the band was over. Decades later collectors found the record, and the accepted history of punk had to make room for it.

hero.alt: Three young men on a paved forecourt outside a white clapboard building lettered TAYLORE AND SONS LIMITED. The man on the left wears a t-shirt reading DEATH; the man in the centre wears a red knitted cap and points at the camera; the man on the right, in an orange t-shirt, looks down at his cupped hands.

body.text: In the mid-1970s, three brothers in Detroit made a record that almost nobody heard. Bobby Hackney played bass and sang. David played guitar. Dannis played drums. They called themselves Death, pressed 500 copies of a single, and then, a few years later, the band was gone. The record was “Politicians in My Eyes.”

Today, it is difficult to hear it without knowing what came later. The guitar is abrasive, the rhythm section pushes hard, and Bobby's voice sounds impatient with the whole world. It has the velocity and tension we now associate with punk, even though punk, as a defined musical culture, had barely arrived. That is part of what makes the story of Death so strange.

The Hackney brothers grew up in Detroit surrounded by music. They started playing together in 1971, drawing initially from the funk and R&B that was everywhere around them. Then came the louder records. The Who and Alice Cooper were important influences, and David, the oldest brother, began pushing the band toward something much harder and more aggressive. They were not setting out to invent a genre. There wasn't really a genre to invent yet.
David came up with the name Death after the brothers' father was killed by a drunk driver while on his way to help an injured coworker. The name unsettled Bobby and Dannis. David insisted on it.

By 1975, Death had developed a sound of its own and recorded seven songs at United Sound Systems in Detroit. Columbia Records took an interest. There was a potential deal, but the label wanted one thing changed: the name. Death refused. The record contract disappeared.

It is tempting to turn that moment into a perfect rock-and-roll parable, but the rest of the story is less tidy. Death didn't immediately become a legendary underground band. They didn't influence a generation of musicians who were waiting for them to arrive. They simply kept going for a while, made a record, and eventually stopped.

The brothers pressed 500 copies of “Politicians in My Eyes” backed with “Keep on Knocking” on their own Tryangle Records label. The records circulated around Detroit, but Death never found a wider audience. By 1977, the band was finished.

Bobby and Dannis eventually moved to Vermont and played reggae in a group called Lambsbread. David moved back to Detroit in 1982. The seven songs from the United Sound sessions remained largely unknown. David died of lung cancer in 2000. He would not live to see the records become famous.

The rediscovery happened gradually. Interest in private-press records, garage rock and the forgotten edges of punk had grown considerably by the 2000s, and Death began turning up in conversations among collectors and musicians. The band's history also remained close to the family. Bobby and Dannis' sons were musicians themselves, helping reconnect the brothers with recordings that had been sitting outside the usual history of rock.

The 45 got expensive the way rare records do. Copies were reaching around eight hundred dollars by 2008, and the highest sale [Discogs](https://www.discogs.com/master/440990-Death-Politicians-In-My-Eyes) has on record for an original Tryangle pressing is $1,275, in October 2019. Five hundred were made; most of what a collector pays for is the four hundred and ninety-nine they cannot have.
Then, in 2009, Drag City released the seven United Sound recordings as ...For the Whole World to See.

body.alt: The cover of ...For the Whole World to See. On a dark navy ground, a thin pink rule frames a grey photograph of a crowded street. The word DEATH is set across the upper left in heavy black capitals, the A drawn as a solid triangle. A beam in pink and two oranges narrows from the lettering down to the lower right, where a city skyline is rendered in orange, pink and yellow along the bottom edge. The words FOR THE WHOLE WORLD TO SEE run in gold across the lower right.
body.caption: The cover of ...For the Whole World to See, the 2009 Drag City release of the seven United Sound recordings. The single had been out of print for thirty-three years.

body.text: For the first time, people could actually hear the music easily. And the music held up. That matters more than the mythology. “Politicians in My Eyes” doesn't sound like an interesting historical curiosity that happens to have arrived early. It sounds like a band that meant it.

Drag City's copy for the reissue leans on two endorsements, and they are sales copy rather than reporting. Jack White, on first hearing the single: “Ahead of punk, and ahead of their time.” Mos Def, more bluntly: “pre-Sex Pistols, pre-Bad Brains, pre-all that shit, and nobody knows about them.” Both lines were written to move a record. Both are also doing the same work, which is to put Death on a timeline that had never kept a place for them.

The question of whether Death were a punk band is harder to settle. The word itself had not yet acquired the meaning it would have a few years later. Calling them “the first punk band” makes the history cleaner than it really was. What is undeniable is the timing. Three Black brothers in Detroit were making stripped-down, confrontational rock before the genre's familiar geography had been established. The conventional story of punk tends to run through New York and London. Death doesn't erase that history, but it makes it considerably less complete.

The rediscovery also brought a second life to the band. Bobby and Dannis eventually began performing again, carrying Death's music forward without David. In 2012, the story reached an even larger audience with A Band Called Death, a documentary by Mark Christopher Covino and Jeff Howlett. The film followed the brothers from Detroit to Vermont and back through the history of the band, the years in Lambsbread, the rediscovery of the recordings and the eventual reunion.

The sons are on the records now too. In November 2023 Drag City released a [split seven inch](https://deathfromdetroit.bandcamp.com/album/death-rough-francis-split) shared between Death and Rough Francis, Death taking “World in Disguise” and Rough Francis “Haunted.” Urian Hackney produced it, Julian Hackney played guitar, and both Bobby Hackneys sing.

There is a tendency with records like this to make the story bigger than the music. The tiny pressing. The failed record deal. The band name. The decades of obscurity. The late recognition. All of it makes for a remarkable story.

But put the needle on the record and the mythology falls away. There are only three brothers playing. The guitar is loud. The drums are relentless. The bass is right underneath it. Bobby sounds furious.

Five hundred copies were made. For decades, almost nobody was listening. Now, “Politicians in My Eyes” is one of those records that seems to have arrived from somewhere slightly outside the official history of rock music. Not because it neatly proves that Death invented punk, but because it demonstrates how much music can exist without anyone paying attention to it.

title: Ken Parker Wrapped a Guitar in Carbon Fibre and Got It Down to Four and a Half Pounds
standfirst: In 1993 Ken Parker wrapped a thin slab of wood in carbon fibre and called it the Fly. Three decades on, nothing else looks like it, and nobody makes it.

hero.alt: David Lynch, in a dark jacket and white shirt, leans against a cracked plaster wall and looks down at the Parker Fly he is playing, in warm sepia light.
hero.caption: David Lynch and his 1997 Parker Fly, posted to his Facebook page in December 2013

_image_provenance: Hero: David Lynch Facebook post, Dec 18 2013, via twinpeaksblog.com. Close-up: Larry Smith for Guitar.com (2022). Catalogue: Parker Guitars 2002 product guide, via Reverb. Weight chart: made for this piece.

body.text: Pick one up and your arm braces for eight pounds but only gets four and a half. The Parker Fly has been doing that to people since 1993. I have dabbled in music, guitar in particular, for decades, yet I had never heard of the Fly until an industrial designer friend of mine raved about it. He called it “the designer's guitar.”

It was the work of two men who spent the better part of a decade arguing about what was wrong with the electric guitar. Ken Parker was a luthier from Long Island who built his first instrument, out of wood and cardboard, at thirteen. Larry Fishman made pickups. They met in 1984.
Their complaint was structural. A solid body guitar is heavy because its wood has two jobs at once: make the sound, and hold the whole thing together against the pull of the strings.

Parker's answer came from the lute, and then from a speedboat. He first tried stiffening a thin body with a hardwood shell. The wood fought him and the results were poor. A friend who built boats out of carbon fibre suggested he try that instead.

The result is best described as an exoskeleton. A slim core of spruce, poplar, basswood or mahogany, glued up, then wrapped in carbon and glass fibre set in epoxy. The skin carries the load. The wood is left free to ring.

Everything else followed from that. With the shell doing the structural work, the neck could melt into the body with almost no heel, and all 24 frets were in easy reach. The fingerboard was composite too, stiff enough that the truss rods added later were widely taken as reassurance for sceptical buyers rather than a necessity.

The frets were stainless steel, glued on rather than hammered in, well before stainless became a selling point anywhere else. The vibrato was Parker's own design on a flat spring. It could float, dive only, or be locked down as a hardtail.

body.alt: Close-up of a silver Parker Fly body on a black background: stainless steel frets, three pickups, the vibrato arm curving over the strings, four black control knobs and two toggle switches, with a cable plugged into the side.
body.caption: Stainless frets, Parker’s vibrato arm, the magnetic pickups and the separate piezo controls, all on one slim silver body.

body.text: Then there was Fishman's half. Alongside two magnetic humbuckers sat a piezo pickup in the bridge, and the player could blend the two or send each to its own amp. Electric, and something close to acoustic, from one guitar at the flick of a switch. When the Fly launched it was billed as the first six-string to mix them.

body.alt: Horizontal bar chart of weight in pounds: the Parker Fly at about 4.5, a typical full-size solid body guitar at 7 to 9 or more.
body.caption: Roughly half the weight of the guitars it was competing with. Figures are approximate and vary by model and wood.

body.text: Nobody had to be told it looked strange. The long upper horn curls forward like driftwood, and the headstock is barely there. One early admirer told Parker it looked like he had found it on a beach, and also like it came from outer space.

Players cared less about the look than about what it did. Joni Mitchell became its most famous owner, on a Fly Concert that was reportedly a factory second pulled from a pile at the Massachusetts shop. Parker fixed it up and fitted a Roland hexaphonic pickup so a VG-8 processor could give her alternate tunings without touching the pegs. She wanted something light. She got it.

Adrian Belew, who went on to a signature model, said Parker had spent twenty years eliminating everything that normally goes wrong with an electric guitar. “I swear this guitar never goes out of tune.”

Dave Navarro used the piezo to jump between the acoustic and distorted halves of “My Friends” live during his Red Hot Chili Peppers years. Matt Bellamy played one on Muse's early tours and on “Thoughts of a Dying Atheist.” Reeves Gabrels, Vernon Reid, Trent Reznor and Eddie Van Halen all turned up with one at some point. David Lynch played his flat across his lap, a 1997 Fly wired to a Roland synth box, changing chords with his feet.

The company around the guitar had a less settled life. Fender was among the firms that looked the design over first. Parker Guitars went to market instead under Korg USA, building Flys in Wilmington, Massachusetts. In 2003 it was sold to U.S. Music Corp., and Ken Parker left that September. The factory moved to the Chicago suburbs.

body.alt: Cover of the Parker Guitars Product Guide 2002: a black and white photo of Ken Parker, bearded with a long braid and glasses, seated on stacked lumber in his workshop and holding an amber Parker Fly, the only thing in colour. Unfinished guitar necks stand in a rack behind him.
body.caption: Ken Parker on the cover of the 2002 Parker Guitars product guide, a year before he left the company.

body.text: Collectors still divide the guitars at that line. The Ken Parker years are “pre-refined”; what came after is “refined.” The changes piled up, and by 2010 the MaxxFly had a conventional headstock, a tamer horn, 22 frets and a slightly heavier body.

Jam Industries of Montreal bought U.S. Music in 2009. In 2015 it announced that American production had stopped and that it was looking for a factory overseas. By November 2016 the Illinois plant was closed. No new Fly has been made since, and the trademarks sit quietly with a division of Jam.

Parker went back to archtops, the jazz guitars he had loved first, building a handful a year by hand with the same mix of old wood and new ideas. He died at home in Gloucester, Massachusetts, on October 5, 2025. He was 73.
The Fly was never going to replace the Stratocaster. It was an argument, made in carbon, that the guitar was not finished.

You can still find one, if you know where to look. The Metropolitan Museum of Art holds [an early prototype](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/671509) in rattle-can silver, carrying the first of Parker's stainless frets. The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History holds a 1997 Fly Classic.

The rest turn up on Reverb and eBay, and now and then at auction. Lynch's Fly sold at Julien's in June 2025 for $32,500, against an estimate of $4,000 to $6,000. A clean Deluxe from the 1990s was fetching around $3,000 to $3,500 a couple of years ago, and the early guitars are the ones people want.
Belew and Gabrels still play theirs. A group of owners runs the Fly Clone Project, documenting every change the guitar went through so that it can be repaired, and perhaps one day built again.
Pick one up if you get the chance. Your arm will make the same mistake.

title: Teenage Engineering’s Real Product Was Always the Company
standfirst: Teenage Engineering has opened a department store on Lafayette Street, and its founder has just said he plans to stop making synthesizers. For twenty years the company has built objects arguing that the object is not the point. He has finally said it out loud.

hero.alt: A black box sign on a brick facade, lettered in white: Teenage Engineering Department Store, 216 Lafayette St, New York.
hero.caption: The sign over the door at 216 Lafayette Street.

body.text: On the upper floor of Teenage Engineering’s new shop at 216 Lafayette Street, there is a working production line. The company’s own staff installed it, and for several weeks after the opening a visitor can walk up and assemble an EP-133 K.O. II sampler by hand.
Think about what that is. A shop with a production line in it is not selling the sampler. It is selling the half hour in which you built the sampler. The object you carry out is a receipt.

body.alt: Visitors in a white-painted brick room under a long pitched skylight, watching staff at a row of workbenches with assembly and test machines, lamps and monitors.
body.caption: The production line upstairs, under the skylight.

body.text: The store opened to invited guests on October 7th and to everyone else this week. Six thousand square feet across two floors, which is the technicality on which the company calls it a department store, a joke delivered with a completely straight face. There was no outside architect: Teenage Engineering designed and built the place itself, fittings included. Upstairs there are workshops and tutorials run by its own people. On the opening night Lykke Li played, and the performance was cut straight to vinyl in the room, on the company’s own machine.

body.alt: Seen from above, a man in a cap and headphones stands at a black vinyl cutting lathe as a clear record turns on its platter, while a visitor in a denim jacket watches.
body.caption: Cutting vinyl in the room

body.text: Almost nothing about that is retail. It is a building that sells the company.

body.alt: A row of OB-4 Magic Radios with carry handles in cream, grey, yellow, orange and red on a long white shelf, in front of lit panels showing a large speaker graphic. Beyond them, a wall of glazed white relief tiles with hands, umbrellas, triangles and discs.
body.caption: OB-4 Magic Radios

body.text: Two days earlier, Highsnobiety had published [an interview](https://www.highsnobiety.com/p/teenage-engineering-interview/) by Lukas Mauve with Jesper Kouthoofd, who co-founded Teenage Engineering in 2005 and runs it. Mauve had gone to the Stockholm headquarters and sat with him on black floor chairs, and came away with the sentence that caught fire on the internet inside a day: during a reorganisation last autumn, Kouthoofd told his staff he plans to stop making synthesizers.
“Everyone was like, ‘What are you talking about?’” he said.

It sounds like a contradiction: a company opens a store the same week its founder says he is done with synthesizers. It isn’t. The store and the interview say the same thing, one in a building and one out loud. Kouthoofd put it more plainly than anyone has since: “I’ve come to the conclusion that, for us, the products aren’t the business.” The real value, he said, “lies in the company as a whole.”

body.alt: A large backlit print of two young men in dark jackets standing in front of stacked racks of glowing equipment, mounted on a wall of the store above a dark rubber floor. A folded stroller stands in front of it.
body.caption: Stroller parking at the entry banner

body.text: Teenage Engineering was founded in Stockholm in 2005 by Kouthoofd, David Eriksson, Jens Rudberg and David Möllerstedt. Three of them had just spent four years running a games company, Netbabyworld. Möllerstedt had run the audio department at EA DICE. Kouthoofd had also been one of the founders of Acne Studios. The company that would define two decades of music hardware came out of video games and fashion, and not out of instrument manufacturing, which is the first clue that the instruments were never the plan.

The OP-1 was built in his garage, shown at NAMM in 2010 and shipping in 2011: a slab of aluminium the size of a paperback, a one-octave keyboard of plastic nubs, a tiny colour screen, and no ancestor anywhere in the synthesizer world. It won a Design S award in 2012 and came second at Georgia Tech’s Guthman competition in 2014.

body.alt: The original Teenage Engineering OP-1 seen from above: a slim pale grey aluminium body with a speaker grille, a small black screen showing a tape reel, four coloured knobs in blue, green, white and orange, rows of round buttons and a two-octave keyboard of flat grey keys.
body.caption: The original OP-1, first shipped in 2011.

body.text: It travelled further than anyone expected. Beck, Jean-Michel Jarre, Depeche Mode and Bon Iver all used one, and by the company’s [own account](https://teenage.engineering/products/op-1/original/anniversary/made-on-op-1) the lead on Usher’s “Scream” was made on it. Hans Zimmer played the Interstellar theme on an OP-1 beside a 1903 Bechstein piano. San Francisco’s Museum of Modern Art keeps one in its permanent collection.

Kouthoofd has always described it as a protest, specifically against making music on a laptop. He is also disarmingly blunt about who buys one: “99% percent of people who buy synths don’t use them as a productive tool for making music.” He calls the OP-1 therapy, entertainment, a hobby. The first version shipped without an undo button, which is either a defect or the entire thesis.
What followed reads less like a product line than a run of position papers.

The OD-11 in 2014, a wireless speaker built on a 1974 Sonab design and made with the Stig Carlsson Foundation: a reissue as a critical argument. The Pocket Operators from 2015, calculator-sized instruments with the circuit board left bare and no case at all, made with the fashion label Cheap Monday and sold for a fraction of an OP-1.

The I-1 for The Impossible Project in 2016, the OP-Z in 2018, and the IKEA FREKVENS range the same year, modular speakers and lights at IKEA prices. The crank on Panic’s Playdate in 2019, probably the most widely owned piece of Teenage Engineering design in the world. The OB-4 in 2020, a radio that continuously records what it plays so you can scrub back through hours of broadcast.

The entire visual language of Nothing from 2021, then the TX-6 and OP-1 field in 2022, the TP-7 and EP-133 K.O. II in 2023, the OP-XY and the Rabbit r1 in 2024, the EP-40 Riddim and the EP-2350 Ting microphone in 2025.

Speakers, radios, cameras, headphones, mixers, recorders, microphones, a games console crank, a phone company’s design identity, an aluminium toy car. The synthesizers were never the business. They were the most famous department of it, which turns out to be a different thing, and a more dangerous one.

body.alt: A lightbox showing a row of small wooden CH-8 Choir figures, each with a speaker or microphone grille, with the real figures lined up on a shelf beneath it against white-painted brick.
body.caption: CH-8 Choir

body.text: The clearest case is the Computer-2. Kouthoofd wanted the PC case to sell for ten dollars and was told that was impossible, because it cost ten dollars to make. So the company gave it away free, which removed the argument rather than winning it. He is explicit that this is the method: “I want to make objects that comment on, or raise questions about, why we accept things as they are.” And, flatly, “We shouldn’t make profits out of the products.”

That is a strange thing for a chief executive to say about a company with roughly a hundred employees and about 46 million dollars in annual revenue. He says it anyway. He concedes the company has “a lot of haters,” partly on price, partly because it sets out to “disturb people’s minds.” He describes the firm as a “democratic organism” that nonetheless needs “a strong voice that can say yes or no,” and he is that voice, personally deciding which prototypes ship. His stated goal for the place is that nobody there is ever bored. “What’s the point of going to work, if it isn’t fun?”
Here is where the theme closes on itself. What Kouthoofd gave Mauve was a statement of philosophy. What the press printed was a product announcement.

Look at what is missing from the interview. There is no company statement; he told his own staff something internally and then repeated it to a journalist. There is no timeline, and the only timing he offers points the other way, at projects that will not surface for five to ten years. There is no list of what counts as a synthesizer, which at this catalogue is a serious problem: the OP-XY is a sequencer, the EP-133 is a sampler, and the line between those and a synth is a category the company has spent twenty years refusing. And there is nothing about the existing range, no discontinuation, no last order date, no word on support. The flat claim that the OP-1 is “no exception” is the writer’s framing, not a quotation.

Then watch it travel. Highsnobiety’s headline said “is going to stop.” Resident Advisor’s said “to stop making synthesisers.” Gearnews softened it to “wants to stop.” Others hardened it into “says it’s done” and “to cease synth production,” asserting a corporate decision nobody has reported. Peter Kirn at [CDM](https://cdm.link/end-of-teenage-synths/) was the only one to push: he asked Teenage Engineering for comment and got nothing, says the larger technology outlets got nothing either, and offers the obvious alternative reading, that Kouthoofd may have reorganised the synthesizer division rather than abolished it. His verdict is that it is “unclear whether we should even worry about that statement.”

An intention described once in a Stockholm office became, inside twenty-four hours, a discontinuation notice. The industry could not hear “the products aren’t the business” as anything other than “the products are ending.”

Which is exactly his complaint, demonstrated at speed and at scale. For twenty years Teenage Engineering has been mistaken for a synthesizer manufacturer that happens to have good taste. Kouthoofd’s view is that it is a company whose output happens, sometimes, to be synthesizers.

body.alt: A visitor in headphones and a long olive coat patches cables into a large synthesizer panel mounted on a tilted aluminium stand on wheels.
body.caption: Patch panel on the upper floor

body.text: So the shop on Lafayette Street is not a monument to the objects, and the timing is not awkward. It is a six thousand square foot room with no outside architect, a stage where a performance becomes a physical record while you watch, a floor of workshops teaching you to use things you need not buy, and a production line where you build the product yourself.
None of it moves units. All of it sells the company. The store is the argument, already built, and not waiting for the synthesizer question to be settled.
